item.title: Nightmare becomes reality as Mississippi State confirms QB Kamario Taylor is out for the season
item.description: Kamario Taylor reportedly faces season-ending toe surgery after a specialist visit, leaving Mississippi State without its breakout sophomore quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi State's worst fears have unfortunately come to fruition as quarterback Kamario Taylor will miss the remainder of the Bulldogs' season due to injury.

Mississippi State issued a statement on Tuesday confirming earlier reports that the signal caller would be sidelined for the rest of 2026 due to "a foot injury that requires surgery." ESPN reported that the season-ending surgery will be performed on his toe.

Taylor injured his toe during Mississippi State's win over Missouri on Sept. 26.

OHIO STATE QB JULIAN SAYIN'S INJURY MAY COMPLETELY RESHAPE THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RACE

The Mississippi native played through the injury in State's 56-23 loss to Alabama on Oct. 3, a game in which he threw for 258 yards, three touchdowns and two interceptions. The Bulldogs then went into their bye week before playing at LSU on Oct. 17, a game Taylor did not suit up for, and one State was shut out 31-0.

Taylor started under center for the Bulldogs against Oklahoma on Oct. 24, but threw just five passes before being sidelined and later leaving the field in a walking boot on his right foot. The Bulldogs fell at home to the Sooners 23-15.

"Over the last few weeks, I've worked every day with our medical staff and done everything possible to be out there with my teammates," Taylor said in a statement.

"Missing the rest of this season is hard to accept, but I know God has a plan. I love this team and I love Mississippi State."

It's not an overreaction to say that Taylor being shelved for the rest of the year is among the most detrimental news any Power Four program in the country could be dealt.

Taylor, a sophomore, began the season putting up Heisman Trophy-type numbers with 15 total touchdowns, 1,192 passing yards, and just two interceptions over the course of the Bulldogs' first four games of the season.

Mississippi State was not only on track to become the most surprising team in the SEC, but around the sport in general, mostly due to Taylor's NFL-caliber arm and freakishly fast start to the year.

In the early stages of the season, one could easily make the argument that the two best quarterbacks in college football happened to be residing in the state of Mississippi, with Taylor in Starkville and Trinidad Chambliss under center for Ole Miss in Oxford.

With Taylor done for the year, Mississippi State will likely lean on Parker Puckett, a redshirt freshman who walked onto the program. Puckett has completed 64 percent of his 64 passes this season, thrown for one touchdown, and a pair of interceptions.

item.title: Haitian national charged with murdering estranged wife outside Walmart after green card marriage goes awry
item.description: Destino Jean Louis allegedly hid near a bush outside the Walmart where his estranged wife worked, waiting for her shift to end before the fatal shooting.
item.content:encoded:
Haitian national Destino Jean Louis was charged with murder after he allegedly killed his wife outside a Pennsylvania Walmart store where she worked following the collapse of their marriage, according to court documents and a press release from the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office.

U.S. Marshals arrested Jean Louis on Friday morning in Philadelphia on charges related to overstaying his visa, which he had originally obtained through a now-terminated relief program for Haitian nationals. The district attorney's office then charged him in connection with the murder while he was in federal custody, authorities said.

"At 9 AM on Friday, October 23rd, Destino Jean Louis, 23, was arrested by [U.S. Marshals Service Philadelphia] on the 6600 block of N. 18th St for immigration violations. Louis, a Haitian national who overstayed his visa, was the prime suspect in the October 21st fatal shooting of a 45 year-old Walmart employee who had just left her shift," U.S. Marshals Service Philadelphia wrote in a Monday post on X.

ICE ARRESTS SOUTHWEST AIRLINES FLIGHT ATTENDANT IN NASHVILLE FOR ALLEGEDLY OVERSTAYING VISA SINCE 2021

Jean Louis' victim, identified by authorities as 45-year-old Latosha Ann Cooper, was his estranged wife whom he had married in March. Investigators told Fox29 that immigration officials had determined the marriage to be not legitimate and was only for immigration purposes.

AMERICAN WOMAN MASTERMINDS $6 MILLION MARRIAGE FRAUD SCHEME, DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE SAYS

In July, Cooper withdrew her petition to sponsor Jean Louis' visa, according to documents reviewed by Fox29.

Jean Louis allegedly hid near a bush outside of the Walmart where Cooper worked, wearing a mask, and waited for her to end her night shift, according to Montgomery Country District Attorney Kevin Steele.

CALIFORNIA WOMAN CHASED, FATALLY SHOT BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DOORDASH DRIVER WHO STALKED HER FOR MONTHS: DHS

"When Cooper left the store, he ran towards her and fatally shot her," according to court documents.

Court filings also revealed that Jean Louis, a former employee at the same Walmart who was terminated for immigration reasons, had previously physically assaulted Cooper and repeatedly contacted store staff to request Cooper's work schedule.

Prosecutors also determined from phone records that Jean Louis had taken multiple trips between his residence in Philadelphia and the Walmart location in Cheltenham in the weeks leading up to the shooting, the documents stated.

Jean Louis is being charged with murder in the first degree, murder in the third degree, illegal alien use of a firearm, carrying a firearm without a license and possession of an instrument with intent to commit a crime, according to court documents.

Fox News Digital contacted the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office for further information.

Jean Louis is being held without bail at the Montgomery County Correctional Facility, per court documents.

item.title: Colts trade Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to Seahawks, the first of what could be multiple deadline moves
item.description: Quenton Nelson's trade to the Seattle Seahawks signals a broader Indianapolis Colts teardown, with DeForest Buckner and Jonathan Taylor also on the block.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts appear to be waving a white flag on the 2026 season, with the first sign coming Tuesday when they traded perennial Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks.

The Seahawks are giving up a third-round pick in the 2027 draft and a fifth-round pick in the 2028 draft for Nelson — a 30-year-old anchor of the Indianapolis offensive line who has been selected to eight Pro Bowls in each of his previous eight seasons.

And this makes sense on multiple levels.

SEAHAWKS DOMINATE CHIEFS 20-3 AS SAM DARNOLD SILENCES CRITICS IN POTENTIAL SUPER BOWL PREVIEW

The Colts are struggling through a disappointing season where they find themselves with a 2-5 record and mired in a three-game losing skid. They've already fired general manager Chris Ballard and the next general manager will need draft capital to rebuild a veteran team that gave up multiple first-round picks last year at the trade deadline for cornerback Sauce Gardner.

The Seahawks, meanwhile, are coming off an impressive victory over the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs and are taking an opportunity to upgrade their offensive line as they try to defend their Super Bowl title.

With Nelson coming aboard, the club will likely move 2025 first-round pick Grey Zabel from left guard to right guard where he played in college at North Dakota State.

The Colts will not admit this is a garage sale. That would be frowned upon by the NFL.

But everyone knows. As recently as the weekend, the wife of running back Jonathan Taylor said her family is on "a Colts transaction watch," signaling Taylor and other players are aware of the current uncertain situation in Indianapolis.

OutKick and Fox News Digital included Nelson's name among the Colts players who could be trade targets before the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline.

item.title: Britain's sweeping new crackdown on 'antisocial' behavior sparks free speech backlash: 'Peak insanity'
item.description: Shabana Mahmood unveiled respect orders, giving courts power to impose curfews and unlimited fines and ban offenders from town centers in England and Wales.
item.content:encoded:
The United Kingdom introduced new "respect orders" across England and Wales on Monday, giving authorities expanded powers to crack down on persistent "antisocial" behavior and drawing criticism from free speech advocates concerned about potential government overreach.

The U.K. government’s order enables police and councils to take stronger "enforcement action" against "adult offenders" of persistent "antisocial" behavior, according to a government news release.

Under the new restrictions, U.K. courts could ban offenders from town centers or prohibit them from drinking in "public hot spots" like local parks, the announcement states. Courts can impose restrictions and requirements through a civil Respect Order, while individuals who breach an order without a reasonable excuse can face criminal prosecution, including potentially unlimited fines or imprisonment.

Under the legislation governing the Respect Orders, antisocial behavior is defined as conduct that has caused, or is likely to cause, harassment, alarm or distress to any person. The definition has prompted concerns from critics that the powers could be applied too broadly, although the law requires judicial approval before an order can be imposed.

UK PRIME MINISTER SAYS FOOTBALL FANS 'SINGLED OUT' BY ALCOHOL BAN NOT IMPOSED ON RUGBY MATCHES

"Unchecked, antisocial [behavior] blights our communities," Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "But it is not inevitable, and I won’t accept it. For too long, we have lacked the powers we need to deal with this problem properly. From today, that changes: authorities will be able to take tough action against these offenders.

"This delivers on a commitment we made to the British people in our manifesto," Mahmood continued. "And, most importantly, those who make life a misery for others will now face the consequences of their actions."

Some offenders may be required to "tackle" the "root causes" of their behavior by participating in drug or alcohol treatment or anger-management programs, according to the announcement.

Violating a respect order is considered a criminal offense, giving police the power to arrest anyone on charges of violating the rules, according to the press release. Those who defy an order could also face up to two years of jail time.

When reached for comment, the U.K. Cabinet Office referred Fox News Digital to the Home Office, which could not immediately be reached for comment.

Alan Mendoza, co-founder and executive director of U.K.-based think tank the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital Tuesday that "vague" definitions under the government's respect orders could result in such enforcement actions being wrongfully "applied to lawful speech or protest."

"I think the breadth of these orders deserves scrutiny, particularly in the case of potentially unlimited fines," Mendoza explained. 

"The government has a legitimate duty to tackle genuinely antisocial behaviour, but the powers need to be tightly defined and proportionate. Vague or elastic definitions could allow measures intended for serious nuisance or harassment to be applied to lawful speech or protest. We have already seen similar after all with social media posts and police investigations that follow.

"There should be clear statutory limits, proper evidence requirements, judicial oversight and an effective right of appeal," he added. "Online criticism, however unwelcome, should not be treated as antisocial [behavior] simply because it is unpopular or embarrassing to those in authority."

UK POLICE APOLOGIZE TO 'FATHER TED' CREATOR GRAHAM LINEHAN FOR ARREST OVER TRANS SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

Mendoza said the U.K. government "should be able to demonstrate that these powers are necessary and contain adequate safeguards against arbitrary or disproportionate use."

The orders notably replace civil injunctions for adult offenders and grant U.K. police more enforcement powers, "including the ability to arrest anyone who breaches an order," according to the announcement.

The new restrictions have drawn intense criticism across social media, with one X user claiming in a post Monday that the orders are "mental," while another X account referred to the rules as "peak insanity."

"Laugh all you want at what a joke England has become, but understand that the U.S. will follow right behind if Democrats ever take full power again," the Federalist CEO and co-founder Sean Davis wrote Monday in an X post.

Tech and free speech lawyer Preston Byrne similarly took to social media to criticize the orders, saying that U.K. residents should "keep in mind that one can cause 'harassment, alarm, or distress' in England and Wales by uttering a true statement of fact to someone who doesn't want to hear it, or by offering an honestly-held opinion or belief, spoken or written, which also offends."

British political commentator Calvin Robinson wrote in an X post Monday responding to the orders that "this tyranny must end."

The U.K. has notably enacted a spate of laws restricting free speech in recent years, including the 2023 Online Safety Act, which gives the country's regulator the authority to impose major fines on digital platforms if they fail to comply with certain requirements.

The new restrictions come amid growing tensions across Europe, where protests and riots have rocked countries, most notably France.

item.title: Serbia’s student movement topples Vucic’s party after 14 years, but political agenda remains unclear
item.description: Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List after a landslide victory ended his 14-year rule over Serbia in a historic election day.
item.content:encoded:
Serbia’s longtime leader, President Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat Sunday to the student-led opposition in an election that sent shock waves throughout Europe and the Western Balkans.

"We do not have the final results yet, and many people will be surprised. Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost these elections. The student-led protest list has won," Vucic said in an address to the nation Sunday night.

The Student List victory brings an end to 14 years of Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party rule, in what many are saying is the biggest political shake-up in the Balkans since the toppling of Yugoslav dictator Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. 

Observers say the Student List party's policies remain vague, which has some worried about Serbia's future.

Ana Brnabic, vice president of the main Board of the Serbian Progressive Party, told Fox News Digital that, "The election victory of the Student List recalls similar electoral triumphs in other countries. The Student List represents a classical anti-establishment movement: it had neither a program nor a coherent political ideology. In an essentially anarchic fashion, it opposed everything, claiming to fight for justice and against corruption."

ANTI‑CORRUPTION PROTESTS HIT EUROPEAN NATION AS CALLS FOR NEW ELECTIONS GROW

She added, "After 14 years of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) rule, people may have wanted change. That is understandable and logical. But the grim consequences of this movement in power will soon become apparent."

Turnout reached 69 %, the highest this century, with more than 4.4 million people casting their ballots, according to Rasa Nedeljkov, head of the CRTA Election Observation Mission.

"This is by all means a historic victory and indeed a surprise to many. While it was clear from the beginning that the students will have an impressive result, very few expected a landslide," Helena Ivanov, associate fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital.

The Election Observation Mission reported that the Student List won 52.45 % of the vote and is projected to hold 138 of 250 seats in the National Assembly, an absolute majority, allowing it to form a government on its own.

Vucic won 39.2 % and is projected to hold 103 seats.

Supporters celebrated throughout Belgrade and across Serbia as it became clear the Student List won by a larger margin that caught many experts and observers by surprise.

Many claimed they were concerned about the possibility of violence escalating as polls began to close. Almost two hours after polling stations closed, Vucic addressed the nation, confirming his defeat and announcing the peaceful transfer of power.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

Vučić was left playing catch-up, and all his attempts to co-opt, demoralize and fragment the movement failed," Sinisa Vukovic, director of the Global Policy Program at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told Fox News Digital.

The CRTA Election Observation Mission reported that the campaign was marked by the abuse of state resources, pressure on candidates and voters, attempts to bring the media under total government control, and attacks on independent election observers.

Tens of thousands of Serbians volunteered to run and monitor polling stations across the country, and the vote was mostly peaceful.

SERBIA, CAUGHT BETWEEN EUROPE AND RUSSIA, COULD MOVE ONE STEP CLOSER TO NORMALIZING RELATIONS WITH KOSOVO

Student led protests marched in the streets for two years after the deaths of 16 people following the collapse of a railway station in the town of Novi Sad in November 2024. People had taken to the streets, demanding justice for those killed and accountability for anyone responsible for the disaster.

The momentum of nearly two years of street demonstrations culminated in a nationwide movement ready for change. The political novices were able to rally the nation behind a simple message against corruption and state capture.

Serbs across the country embraced the Student List, who are viewed as fresh faces in politics and are not tied to Serbia’s traditional political opposition, which is perceived as ineffective and corrupt by a lot of the voters.

EXCLUSIVE: SERBIAN PRESIDENT VUČIĆ SAYS SUPPORT FOR US 'SURGED' UNDER TRUMP, INVITES HIM TO VISIT BELGRADE

Milos Jevtic, a 48-year-old professor with the Faculty of Organizational Sciences at the University of Belgrade, was among the many Student List candidates who won a seat in parliament.

Jevtic told Fox News Digital that their victory came from the values that the students have stood for from the very beginning: expertise, professionalism, responsibility, solidarity and unity.

"What is particularly important is that the students have never compromised on these values and principles. Of course, widespread public dissatisfaction also played a major role, along with a lack of trust in both the current regime and the opposition parties," Jevtic explained.

Jevtic said he believes the priorities for the new Student List-run government should be economic stability, fighting corruption, establishing the rule of law and strengthening institutions, much of what carried the student-led protests since 2024.

"The ultimate goal is to build a system in which institutions function in the interests of all citizens," Jevtic said.

On foreign policy, there is an expectation that there will be a certain degree of continuity with the Vucic administration in international relations, including maintaining good relations with neighboring European countries and all major international partners.

But Brnabic warned that "Serbia has lost meaningful political pluralism. After 35 years of a multiparty system, the country is effectively left with one established political party, SNS, while the rest of the political scene is dominated by largely unknown movements without a clear ideology. This is catastrophic for any parliamentary democracy."

She added, "Secondly, nobody in Serbia knows where the country is heading. Are we firmly pro-EU? Will we maintain our ties with Russia? What about China? Will we continue to enhance our relations with the United States — which was a priority of Aleksandar Vucic? Will economic policy be more left-liberal or conservative? Are we heading towards a woke liberal society, or will we preserve our traditional Orthodox Christian values? There are no clear answers to any of these questions."

She concluded by noting, "We have also called for Parliament and all state institutions to be constituted as soon as possible, so that the country has functioning institutions on which people can rely. We will be a strong but constructive opposition. We call on the Student List’s representatives to end the intimidation and assume the responsibility entrusted to them by the voters."

item.title: Reporter caught in violent Paris protests recalls how 'all of a sudden, it exploded' after peaceful march
item.description: A New York Post reporter describes how masked newcomers turned a peaceful Paris march of 100,000 into violent chaos as fury rages against the government.
item.content:encoded:
A New York Post reporter caught in the chaos of violent protests in Paris recounted how a peaceful march of more than 100,000 people took a frightening turn.

"All of a sudden, it exploded," Gabrielle Fahmy recalled Tuesday on "Fox & Friends."

"When it got dark, when they reached the endpoint of the march, it's like they didn't know what to do anymore," she continued.

PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE

"Tensions had been mounting. These new people I saw sort of joined the protest towards the end. We saw some people arrive by metro. They were dressed differently, hiding their faces. They had masks, and that's sort of when I could see things start to shift."

Fahmy told co-host Brian Kilmeade the protests were peaceful for several hours, describing the transition from police leading the crowd to violence erupting in the streets as "very surreal."

FIFTY ANTIFA GROUPS IN FRANCE JOIN VAST NETWORK TO ENSURE CHAOS IN WEEKEND PROTESTS

She said the newcomers appeared to be younger demonstrators, many in their late teens and early 20s, and suggested some might have been "factions of the far-left."

The protests began as student-led demonstrations over teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools but have since evolved into a broader anti-government movement, with protesters voicing frustration over the cost of living and other grievances.

"The people there on Saturday, it was a general sort of cost of living that they were complaining about," Fahmy recalled.

"There's not enough jobs, they're not making enough money, they can't afford to put food on the table. But also anti-government, they are fed up with Emmanuel Macron, who's on his way out anyway. But, it was just a very general, general reason."

Fahmy also recalled seeing Palestinian flags, noting that "everybody with a grievance" seemed to have joined the demonstrations.

Separate protests have also turned violent in Rome and Albania's capital, Tirana, where demonstrators set government buildings on fire.

Fox News' James Cirrone and Brittany Miller contributed to this report.
